brief.question: Do AI conversational agents improve depression and psychological distress?
brief.conclusion: Based on 5 decision-eligible record(s) (5 total retrieved) with early overall strength, the available evidence for the question 'Do AI conversational agents improve depression and psychological distress?' indicates studied populations including Mixed populations across 35 experimental studies; older-adult evidence is subgroup evidence; Participants in 12 chatbot mental-health studies; 210 adults recruited nationally for a four-week wait-list trial; University students; mean age 22.9 among completers; Paying Youper users who consented to research use of their data. Documented improved outcomes include: anxiety; depression; feeding and eating disorder risk.  This is a deterministic draft synthesis derived only from stored evidence records.
populations_studied: Mixed populations across 35 experimental studies; older-adult evidence is subgroup evidence
210 adults recruited nationally for a four-week wait-list trial
University students; mean age 22.9 among completers
Paying Youper users who consented to research use of their data
limitations_and_risks: Interventions and populations were heterogeneous; older-adult certainty comes from subgroup evidence rather than an older-adult-only synthesis.
Few studies per outcome, high risk of bias, uncertain clinical importance, and sparse safety assessment prevent firm conclusions.

Wait-list comparison, possible selection toward younger technology-positive participants, paid assessments, only four weeks of postintervention follow-up, and intensive expert safety supervision limit transferability.
A correction published 2026-08-26 removed an unverified chatbot-response example and clarified methodological alignment with the Woebot trial. Original chat transcripts were no longer available.
University sample and short follow-up limit generalization. Several authors were affiliated with X2AI.
Commercial-conflict disclosure: three authors were affiliated with X2AI. The deleted response example must not be used downstream.
Paying-user selection, attrition and lack of randomized comparison limit causal conclusions.
Several authors were affiliated with Youper; older-adult applicability requires separate assessment.

brief.question: Does PRISM improve loneliness and social support for older adults?
brief.conclusion: Based on 5 decision-eligible record(s) (5 total retrieved) with early overall strength, the available evidence for the question 'Does PRISM improve loneliness and social support for older adults?' indicates studied populations including 245 adults aged 64–99 in rural and senior-housing settings; 300 community-dwelling older adults at risk of social isolation; Older adults represented in 25 publications; Participants across the lifespan in seven randomized trials; 646 older adults across six heterogeneous studies. Documented improved outcomes include: no clearly improved outcomes documented.  This is a deterministic draft synthesis derived only from stored evidence records.
populations_studied: 245 adults aged 64–99 in rural and senior-housing settings
300 community-dwelling older adults at risk of social isolation
Participants across the lifespan in seven randomized trials
646 older adults across six heterogeneous studies
limitations_and_risks: Nine-month data were disrupted by COVID-19, outcomes varied by living context, and common training/contact may explain improvement in both groups.
The bundled system included internet access, training, technical support, and multiple functions, so results cannot isolate one feature or an AI companion.
Searches predated 2016, interventions and measures were heterogeneous, follow-up was often short, and the review cautioned that ICT was not suitable for every older adult.
The review was not older-adult-only, intervention-type moderators could not be tested, and the prediction interval included benefit and harm.
Only six heterogeneous studies were included, searches ended July 2019, and effect estimates were imprecise.

brief.question: What is WHO policy framing for responsible AI health governance?
brief.conclusion: [who-lmm; context] WHO's large multi-modal model guidance identifies health-specific governance needs and cautions that general-purpose model capability is not proof of safe or effective health use. [who-ethics-2021; context] WHO places ethics and human rights at the center of health-AI design, deployment, and use, and sets six consensus principles with governance and accountability recommendations. [who-2025; context] WHO presents social isolation and loneliness as widespread problems with health, well-being and societal consequences, and calls for social health to receive urgency comparable to physical and mental health. [who-2025; context] The report calls for cross-sector action to strengthen social connection, addressing policy-makers, researchers and other sectors. [nist-genai-profile; context] NIST's Generative AI Profile applies Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage to generative-AI risks, emphasizing governance, content provenance, predeployment testing, and incident disclosure. [who-regulatory-2023; context] WHO summarizes regulatory considerations for health AI, including documentation, lifecycle evaluation, risk management, intended use, data quality, privacy, and stakeholder collaboration. These sources provide context, design, or evidence-map findings; they do not establish intervention effectiveness.
limitations_and_risks: This is policy guidance, not an effectiveness evaluation; the publication page date and edition history require explicit version confirmation.
General health-AI guidance does not establish companion effectiveness or a clinical standard of care.
This policy report does not establish the effectiveness of an AI companion.

The profile is voluntary and cross-sector; it identifies risks such as anthropomorphism, automation bias, overreliance, emotional entanglement, confabulation, and privacy without proving a product safe.
WHO explicitly describes the document as a nonexclusive overview, not regulatory guidance, a framework, or an effectiveness source.

brief.question: What design principles address artificial agents and loneliness?
brief.conclusion: [loveys-2019; design] The viewpoint proposes design considerations for artificial agents grounded in attachment, social regulation, and therapeutic-relationship concepts; it is not empirical effectiveness evidence. [skjuve-2021; design] Among 18 interviewees selected because they already had an established chatbot friendship, participants described accepting, understanding, and nonjudgmental responses as factors in relationship development; these are reported perceptions, not proven clinical benefits. [skjuve-2021; design] Effects on users’ wider social context were mixed, and participants reported stigma associated with human–chatbot relationships. These sources provide context, design, or evidence-map findings; they do not establish intervention effectiveness.
limitations_and_risks: This is a conceptual viewpoint without intervention outcomes, so every design statement must be presented as a proposal rather than validated efficacy.
Participants were selected for an existing chatbot friendship; findings cannot represent all users or older adults.
Qualitative self-reports do not establish causal improvements in mental health or loneliness.

brief.question: What evidence gaps exist for digital interventions, loneliness, and older adults?
brief.conclusion: [welch-2023-egm; evidence_map] Searches covered studies published only through May 2021; at the September 2026 review this evidence map is more than five years out of date. Community-level outcomes and process measures are rarely reported. Included work does not assess affordability or lack of accessibility, and adverse effects are seldom reported. [welch-2023-egm; evidence_map] Searches covered studies published only through May 2021; at the September 2026 review this evidence map is more than five years out of date. The map contains 200 articles: 97 systematic reviews and 103 primary studies. Most evidence comes from high-income settings and none from low-income countries. [welch-2023-egm; evidence_map] Searches covered studies published only through May 2021; at the September 2026 review this evidence map is more than five years out of date. More than 70% of the included systematic reviews were rated critically low quality. [marziali-2024; evidence_map] Among 16 voice-assistant studies, loneliness and social isolation were minor themes in most; the review primarily found preliminary positive usability and user-experience results. These sources provide context, design, or evidence-map findings; they do not establish intervention effectiveness.
limitations_and_risks: A map describes coverage and gaps, not a pooled intervention effect.
Searches extended through May 2021; this is not a current exhaustive map.
The review is heterogeneous and only a minority of studies directly measured loneliness or social isolation.
